title: Three Words Aren't Enough: Rethinking Motivation
author: Andrew Watson
summary: Andrew Watson interrogates the popular three-word summary of Deci and Ryan's self-determination theory (SDT) - autonomy, relatedness, competence - arguing that even though the theory has genuine, decades-deep research behind it, reducing it to a checklist formula is a mistake many educators make. His central move is to show that the three needs can directly conflict: offering a struggling student a hint, for example, may build relatedness (the student feels noticed and helped) while simultaneously undermining their sense of autonomy (feeling babied) or competence (feeling incapable), depending on how the individual student experiences it. He extends this with a second example - giving students independent work time, seemingly foundational to good teaching, can build autonomy and competence for well-prepared students while overwhelming and demotivating students who lack the prior knowledge to work productively alone. Watson's broader point is that SDT's headline concepts are an excellent starting place for pedagogical thinking but cannot function as a plug-and-play formula, since any given strategy's effect depends on individual differences, cultural context, and potential trade-offs between the three needs. He closes by generalising this caution to all research-backed teaching strategies: rather than picking one because it 'sounds uplifting and research-y,' teachers should interrogate whether the specific benefit fits their specific students' current needs.
points: Watson's central critique: self-determination theory's headline trio - autonomy, relatedness, competence - is often presented as a simple formula, but the three needs can directly conflict with one another depending on how a specific strategy is experienced by a specific student.

His key illustrative example: offering a struggling student a hint may build relatedness (they feel helped) while simultaneously undermining their autonomy (feeling babied) or competence (feeling incapable) - the same action can cut both ways.

A second example - 'give students time for independent work' - shows the same tension: well-prepared students may feel more autonomous and competent, while students lacking prior knowledge may become overwhelmed and demotivated by the same strategy.

Watson's three follow-up questions for any research-backed motivational strategy: What are the potential conflicts between the Big Three needs? What are the individual differences at play? What are the cultural differences at play?

His broader generalisation beyond SDT: teachers shouldn't adopt a strategy simply because it 'sounds uplifting and research-y' - the real work is asking whether the specific benefit fits the specific students in front of you, weighing upsides against downsides.
quotes: For a few decades now, Richard Deci and Edward Ryan have developed self-determination theory: a theory of academic motivation that gets LOTS of love.
We should start by admitting that LOTS of people who talk about self-determination theory don't get past these headlines.
On the one hand, that advice could certainly foster a sense of relatedness in the classroom... At the same time, offering hints might lessen another student's sense of autonomy.
Yes, you will hear "autonomy! relatedness!! competence!!!" offered as a formula to enhance student motivation. But I don't think this formula -- or ANY formula -- works simply as a formula.
On the other hand, students who lack appropriate prior knowledge could be overwhelmed and demotivated by all that time to work alone.
In other words: if I worry that my students lack motivation, I shouldn't simply look at that list and pick one that sounds uplifting and research-y.
